predictions.title: Open-weight coding model tops 85 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 by Q4 2026
predictions.body: GLM-5.2's fully-open MIT release lands at 81.0 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 62.1 on SWE-bench Pro, trailing the closed frontier's 85.0 by roughly four points while undercutting it on price-performance and already wiring into 20-plus coding environments. Each open-weight generation from the Chinese coding-model labs has closed a chunk of that gap rather than holding station, and the surrounding serving stack is removing the deployment tax that kept these models off local hardware: vLLM v0.23.0 promotes its faster execution path to default for dense models, and MosaicQuant's unified 4-bit scheme reports near-FP16 accuracy, making large MoE weights cheaper to run yourself. The prediction is that a permissively-licensed (MIT or Apache-2.0) open-weight model reaches or exceeds 85.0 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 on vendor-reported scores, erasing the headline coding gap to the closed leader. The score is benchmark-specific and falsifiable; independent replication and production latency remain the open caveats, but the trajectory points at parity on this metric within two quarters.

reasoning.because: GLM-5.2 open weights hit 81.0 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 vs frontier 85.0, a gap closing per release
reasoning.given: Cheaper 4-bit serving (MosaicQuant) and vLLM defaults cut the local-deployment tax on open weights
reasoning.so_that: A permissively-licensed open-weight coding model posts a Terminal-Bench 2.1 score at or above 85.0
reasoning.landing: by Q4 2026; the open-weight lab's own benchmark card reports the crossing
reasoning.plain_language: Free-to-download AI coders are catching up fast. Within about two quarters, one should match the best paid coding model on a key test.

predictions.summary: GLM-5.2's open MIT weights reached 81.0 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 versus 85.0 for the closed frontier, narrowing the coding gap each release while cheaper 4-bit serving lowers the cost of running them locally. Expect a permissively-licensed open-weight model to reach 85.0 on that benchmark by Q4 2026.

predictions.title: Rival humanoid maker lands $500M-plus chip-and-cloud strategic round by Q4 2026
predictions.body: Neura Robotics' Series C of up to $1.4 billion, which surfaced June 10 at a valuation reported near $7 billion, did more than set a robotics fundraising mark: it pulled Nvidia, Amazon, Qualcomm and Bosch directly onto a full-stack humanoid maker's cap table alongside a Tether-led syndicate. That roster signals chip and cloud strategics are now treating equity in humanoid builders as a way to anchor downstream demand for their compute, silicon and fleet-services stacks rather than waiting for arm's-length procurement. With deployment revenue across the humanoid sector still early and several rivals racing toward serial production, the prediction is that at least one other full-stack humanoid company closes a comparably large strategic round, $500 million or more, with at least one of the same chip or cloud strategics participating, by the fourth quarter of 2026.

reasoning.because: Neura Robotics drew a >=$1.4B strategic Series C from Nvidia, Amazon and Qualcomm on June 10
reasoning.given: Chip and cloud strategics now buy direct humanoid cap-table seats to lock compute and fleet demand
reasoning.so_that: A second full-stack humanoid maker closes a comparable round with at least one overlapping chip/cloud strategic
reasoning.landing: by Q4 2026; another humanoid maker round >=$500M with a chip/cloud strategic
reasoning.plain_language: Investors that make AI chips and cloud just put big money into a robot maker, so another robot startup will get a similar deal soon.

predictions.summary: Neura Robotics' up-to-$1.4B Series C put Nvidia, Amazon and Qualcomm directly on a humanoid maker's cap table at a ~$7B valuation. That strategic pattern suggests another full-stack humanoid company will close a $500M-plus round with at least one overlapping chip or cloud backer by Q4 2026.

predictions.title: Enterprises self-host open-weight code models over hosted China APIs by Q2 2027
predictions.body: GLM-5.2's fully-open MIT release is the inflection that turns the open-weight coding-model trend into a data-sovereignty decision rather than just a price-performance one. The weights are publicly downloadable and run on local or virtual-machine hardware, and the surrounding stack now makes self-hosting practical at scale: vLLM v0.23.0 promotes its faster execution path to default for dense models, and MosaicQuant's unified 4-bit scheme reports near-FP16 accuracy, cutting the memory and cost of running a 753B mixture-of-experts yourself. The same coverage that praises the model's price-performance flags the catch: routing requests through Z.ai's hosted API carries China-jurisdiction data-handling considerations that enterprises with sensitive code and regulated data must weigh. That splits the buying decision in two - you can take the open weights and run them inside your own boundary, or consume the convenient hosted API and accept foreign data jurisdiction. The prediction is that within roughly three quarters this hardens into an explicit posture: at least one named enterprise, regulated-sector buyer, or developer-tooling framework publishes guidance or a default that prefers self-hosting permissively-licensed open weights over a foreign-hosted inference API specifically on data-jurisdiction or sovereignty grounds, treating where-the-inference-runs as a procurement control rather than an afterthought. The catalyst is a top-tier open-weight coding model that is genuinely self-hostable arriving at the same moment cheap 4-bit serving removes the deployment tax; the same data-sovereignty thread runs through this month's Confidential Computing Summit agenda. The counter-risk is that managed convenience and tooling integrations keep most teams on the hosted API despite the jurisdiction flag, leaving self-hosting a regulated-sector niche rather than a published default.

reasoning.because: GLM-5.2 ships self-hostable MIT weights; its hosted Z.ai API flags China data-jurisdiction handling
reasoning.given: Cheap 4-bit serving (MosaicQuant) plus vLLM defaults make running the weights yourself a real option
reasoning.so_that: Enterprises codify a self-host-the-weights, avoid-the-foreign-hosted-API posture for sensitive-code data sovereignty
reasoning.landing: by Q2 2027; >=1 enterprise/framework self-host policy cites data jurisdiction
reasoning.plain_language: A top free Chinese AI coder is now downloadable. Firms worried where their code data goes will run it in-house, not its cloud.

predictions.summary: GLM-5.2's open MIT weights are self-hostable, while its hosted Z.ai API carries China data-jurisdiction concerns, and cheaper 4-bit serving makes self-hosting practical. Expect an enterprise or dev-tooling framework to publish a self-host-over-foreign-API policy on sovereignty grounds by Q2 2027.
